title: Counting Teeth Predicted Survival After Cancer Surgery
hook: Among 339 pancreatic cancer patients, those with at least 21 natural teeth lived nearly two years longer after surgery. Teeth are standing in for something bigger.
key_points: In a study of 339 pancreatic cancer patients, those with 21+ natural teeth survived nearly two years longer post-surgery.
The researchers don't argue teeth cause survival — they read tooth count as a marker.
Tooth loss can reflect decades of chronic inflammation, poor nutrition, and frailty.
It may also be a rough index of lifetime access to care and general resilience.
Tooth count is cheap and objective, which is exactly what makes it appealing as a prognostic signal.
Observational data — no evidence yet that dental work changes cancer outcomes.
content_html: Here's a prognostic marker no one asks for: how many teeth you have. Among 339 patients who had surgery for pancreatic cancer, those with at least 21 natural teeth survived nearly two years longer than those with fewer.
extra_html:
The researchers are explicit that they don't think teeth are doing the work. Tooth loss is a slow accumulator — it records decades of chronic inflammation, gum disease, nutritional shortfalls, smoking, frailty, and unequal access to dental care. All of those also shape whether someone can withstand a major abdominal operation and the treatment that follows. Tooth count just happens to be a cheap, objective, retrospectively available summary of them.

This is observational, so the practical reading is careful: it does not show that dental work improves cancer outcomes. What it does support is the broader theme this deck keeps returning to — oral health is not a separate compartment from the rest of the body's condition. Good gum health is worth having on its own terms, and a clinician who notices extensive tooth loss is looking at a patient who may need more support, not just a dentist.

related.title: Why Oral Health Matters
related.hook: Your mouth isn't sealed off from the rest of you. Gum disease and untreated decay are linked to problems well beyond the teeth — and most of it is preventable.

related.title: A Hidden Heart Valve Risk Linked to Gum Disease
related.hook: Gum disease is already linked to heart disease in general — new research points to a specific mechanism: bacteria that may help trigger a serious, calcium-driven heart valve condition.

related.title: Brushing and Flossing, Done Right
related.hook: Brushing twice a day sounds obvious — but for two minutes, with fluoride, and adding daily flossing, is where most people quietly fall short.

related.title: A Drug for 'Undruggable' Pancreatic Cancer
related.hook: A new drug, daraxonrasib, hits a KRAS mutation long thought 'undruggable' and nearly doubled survival in a trial of advanced pancreatic cancer — a hard-to-treat disease.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the researchers think tooth count tracked survival?

choices.text: Teeth act as a marker of decades of inflammation, nutrition, and frailty
Teeth directly help the body fight pancreatic tumors
Patients with more teeth received different chemotherapy

flashcards.explanation_html: The argument is proxy, not cause. Losing teeth reflects long-running inflammation, nutritional status, frailty, and access to care — the same factors that shape how well someone withstands major surgery.

flashcards.prompt: What was the cutoff and the size of the difference?
flashcards.back_html: Patients with at least 21 natural teeth survived nearly two years longer after surgery than those with fewer, in a study of 339 people.

flashcards.prompt: What can't you conclude from this study?
flashcards.back_html: That dental treatment improves cancer survival. It's observational — tooth count predicted the outcome; nobody showed that changing it changes the outcome.
